scenes.scene_goal: The investigator arrives at Graymouth Pier in the early evening.
scenes.scene_description: The investigator arrives at Graymouth Pier in the early evening. Rain taps against the warehouses, fishing boats knock against their ropes, and the lighthouse beam across the water is turning at an irregular rhythm. Constable Mara Vale waits beside a locked gate, a folded oilskin coat, and a damp crate marked by tidewater. The opening should make three natural approaches visible without solving them: question Vale, inspect the abandoned coat and crate, or ask to pass through the gate toward the lighthouse launch.

plots.plot_goal: Constable Vale says lighthouse keeper Elias Rook sent one final radio message: "The light is counting backward." She found no blood at the pier, but the lighthouse launch is missing and the keeper's oilskin coat was left folded on a crate.
plots.raw_text:
Constable Vale says lighthouse keeper Elias Rook sent one final radio message: "The light is counting backward." She found no blood at the pier, but the lighthouse launch is missing and the keeper's oilskin coat was left folded on a crate. She is afraid Rook is still alive somewhere cold, and more afraid that the harbor families will call it another accident. She can answer basic questions about Rook, the coat, the launch, the lighthouse, and who last came to the pier. If questioned carefully or reassured, she admits the harbor bell rang five times at 3:17 a.m., even though the bell rope had been removed last winter.

If the investigator asks who else knew Rook's habits, Vale reluctantly mentions Jonah Mercer, owner of the old customs house. Mercer came to the pier two nights ago asking whether Rook had "fixed the order yet," then left before anyone could question him. Vale is slow to mention Mercer because her own family name appears in old lighthouse records; she worries any official report will drag her father into the same old shame. If the player is unsure what to ask next, Vale can naturally offer: "You can question me, look over Rook's coat, or I can unlock the gate so you can see the launch mooring."

plots.plot_goal: The pier boards are slick with rain.
plots.raw_text:
The pier boards are slick with rain. The folded oilskin coat, the crate beneath it, the locked gate, and the empty launch mooring are all visible and safe starting points. A basic inspection reveals the coat is dry inside despite the rain and smells faintly of lamp oil. The crate bears a customs house stamp that does not belong on fresh fishing cargo. A successful search can reveal fresh salt crystals arranged in five small arcs beside the crate. A hard or extreme success also notices that the crystals form the same pattern as the lighthouse lens shutters when they close. The locked gate can be opened by Vale, by force, or by a successful Locksmith-style action.

The gate should not stop the investigation. If Vale opens it, she begins to trust the investigator and answers one extra question honestly. If it is forced, someone in the harbor notices the noise before dawn. If it is opened quietly, the investigator sees that the launch ropes were untied by someone who knew the pier, not cut in panic. Any outcome should leave at least one clear next lead: the lighthouse launch route, the customs house stamp, or another question for Vale.

scenes.scene_goal: The investigator reaches the lighthouse by launch.
scenes.scene_description: The investigator reaches the lighthouse by launch. Inside, the stairwell smells of hot metal and seawater. The lamp room still burns, but the rotation mechanism is jammed by a brass notebook wedged between the gears. It was placed there deliberately, not dropped: Rook was trying to slow the count and leave proof where the next keeper would have to look.

plots.plot_goal: The notebook contains Elias Rook's observations from the past week.
plots.raw_text:
The notebook contains Elias Rook's observations from the past week. He believed the light was no longer warning ships away from rocks; instead, it was signaling something beneath the harbor. Early pages are mundane weather logs, which makes the later fear feel earned rather than theatrical. The final page is written in a shaking hand: "Five flashes, five bells, five names. If the order is broken, it answers."

Two later lines are squeezed into the margin: "Mercer knows which name was removed. He heard the first wrong bell and lived." Beneath that, Rook has written, "Before dawn, one bell may reset the order. After dawn, the light starts counting again." If the player has not found the customs house stamp, the notebook also contains a loose receipt from Mercer's warehouse for lamp oil delivered after midnight.

plots.plot_goal: The lamp room windows are streaked with salt from the inside.
plots.raw_text:
The lamp room windows are streaked with salt from the inside. A careful inspection reveals five names scratched into the metal frame: Rook, Vale, Mercer, Tain, and Sable. The name "Mercer" is crossed out, but the scratched groove is fresh and ragged, unlike the old careful lettering around it. The lens can be stopped safely with a Mechanical Repair or DEX-style action, but a failure causes the light to flare and forces a SAN check.

If the investigator compares the scratched names with the notebook, they can see the names were meant to be read clockwise around the frame, matching the shutter positions. Mercer was not merely crossed out; his name was cut out of sequence. This scene should offer redundant paths forward: the notebook points to Mercer, the fresh scratch shows someone altered the order, and the lamp-oil receipt or customs stamp points back to the old customs house.

scenes.scene_goal: When the lens is stopped or the pattern is understood, the harbor bell rings from below the water.
scenes.scene_description: When the lens is stopped or the pattern is understood, the harbor bell rings from below the water. The missing launch drifts back into view with Elias Rook inside, alive but barely conscious. He points toward the old customs house and whispers, "Mercer answered it first." If helped with First Aid, warmth, or steady questioning, Rook can add that Mercer begged him to remove one name, then panicked when the wrong bell began to ring.

plots.plot_goal: Jonah Mercer, owner of the customs house, knows the five names are the current keepers of an old smuggling pact.
plots.raw_text:
Jonah Mercer, owner of the customs house, knows the five names are the current keepers of an old smuggling pact. He crossed out his own name because his sister's child is the next Mercer who would inherit the duty, and he thought removing his name would spare the family. He did not intend Rook to vanish; he sent Rook to alter the order, then locked the customs house and pretended the harbor could survive one more lie. If pressured with evidence from the notebook or the lamp room, Mercer admits that the bell marks each person who has heard the signal and that Rook is not the first to vanish.

Mercer inherited the pact from his father and tried to erase himself after the last winter disappearance. He starts defensive, offering money and insisting the missing keeper was "already doomed," but guilt makes him brittle. If confronted with the customs house stamp, the crossed-out name, Rook's receipt, or Vale's account of his late visit, he breaks more quickly. He says, "One bell. Five names. Always in order. That was how our fathers kept it sleeping. Five bells is not a warning. Five bells is an invitation."

plots.plot_goal: The signal can be ended by restoring the five-name order and ringing the harbor bell once at dawn, or by destroying the lens before it completes another backward count.
plots.raw_text:
The signal can be ended by restoring the five-name order and ringing the harbor bell once at dawn, or by destroying the lens before it completes another backward count. The quieter solution saves Rook and leaves Mercer to confess. Destroying the lens ends the threat immediately, but the lighthouse burns and Graymouth loses its warning light for the winter.

To restore the order, the investigator must mark Mercer's name back into its proper place on the lamp room frame, speak or read the five names clockwise, and ring the old harbor bell once as dawn reaches the lens. The bell rope is gone, but the bell can be struck from the customs house winch chain, from the lighthouse launch hook, or by any practical tool the investigator brings to the pier. If the player understands the rule but lacks a tool, Mercer can be pushed into revealing the winch chain; this keeps the finale tense without turning it into an inventory dead end.

knowledge.title: Constable Mara Vale
knowledge.content: Mara Vale is practical, exhausted, and protective of the harbor workers. She knows more than she first admits because her family name appears in old lighthouse records. Her main motive is not deceit; she wants Rook saved without making her family the next public scapegoat.

knowledge.title: Elias Rook
knowledge.content: Elias Rook is the missing lighthouse keeper. He is cautious and methodical, and his notebook is the best source of confirmed information about the light. He jammed the mechanism on purpose so someone would find his notes before the backward count finished.

knowledge.title: Jonah Mercer
knowledge.content: Jonah Mercer owns the old customs house. He fears the signal and wants to survive more than he wants to tell the truth. His selfishness has a human root: he tried to save his family from an inherited duty and made the whole harbor more dangerous.

knowledge.title: Graymouth Harbor
knowledge.content: Graymouth Harbor is an aging fishing port with a lighthouse, a fog bell, a locked pier gate, and an abandoned customs house. The harbor has a history of smuggling and disappearances during winter storms.

knowledge.title: Fivefold Pattern
knowledge.content: The repeated number five connects the bell rings, salt arcs, scratched names, and lens shutter positions. The clue is obtained by comparing evidence from the pier and lighthouse.

knowledge.title: Ending the Signal
knowledge.content: The signal is reset by one bell, five names, and the correct clockwise order before dawn. Rook's notebook gives the timing, the lamp room gives the order, and Mercer can explain the old rule if pressured with evidence.

script_summary: This short demo is a grounded investigative mystery for one player. The player is an investigator called to the old harbor district after a lighthouse keeper sends a strange message and vanishes before dawn.
